readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 1: Clutch and Kind
readings.challenge: Listen for what each brother’s name tells you about him.
readings.focus: Two shepherd brothers, one grasping and one gentle, and a flock that begins to disappear.
readings.context: From Frances Browne’s Granny’s Wonderful Chair (1857), a book of fairy tales. A girl named Snowflower has a magic chair that tells stories when she asks it, and this is one of them. Because the chair is speaking, every paragraph begins with a quotation mark, and the people in the story speak inside single quotation marks. A shepherd looks after sheep with a crook, a hooked stick, and a pipe, a simple flute. Sheep are sheared, or clipped, with shears like big scissors, to take their wool, which grows back. A ewe is a mother sheep. Covetous means always wanting more for yourself. A dispute is an argument, and the folding is when sheep are shut in their pen at night.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from the start to the sheep beginning to stray; opens “"Once upon a time there lived in the south country two brothers, whose business it was to…”; closes “…to go; and, count the flock when they might, some were sure to be missed at the folding.”.

questions.prompt: What are the two brothers called? How do the names fit them?
facilitatorNotes: Clutch, who grabs and holds on to everything for himself, and Kind, who would share his last bite with a hungry dog.
evidence: one of whom was called Clutch, and the other Kind
Kind would have shared his last morsel with a hungry dog

questions.prompt: What happens after the traders praise Clutch’s wool and pay the highest price?
facilitatorNotes: He clips the sheep closer and more often, leaving them bare even when the days turn cold.
evidence: he left the poor sheep as bare as if they had been shaven

questions.prompt: Why does Kind not quarrel with Clutch over their father’s sheep?
facilitatorNotes: He would rather keep the peace than fight for sheep, so he works as a helper. Some children will think he should stand up for himself; he does argue later, for the sheep.
evidence: Kind wouldn't quarrel with his brother for the sake of the sheep

questions.prompt: Which sheep are the first to go missing? What might that mean?
facilitatorNotes: The closest clipped. Perhaps the cold, bare sheep are leaving, or something is taking them away from a greedy master. The story has not said yet; let children guess.
evidence: the closest clipped were the first to go

readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 2: Up the hills
readings.challenge: Watch where Kind looks when he is sad, and what he sees there.
readings.focus: With nothing left, the brothers climb the hills no shepherd has crossed, and music leads them to a wonder.
readings.context: Recap: Clutch, the greedy elder brother, clipped his sheep so close and so often that they shivered bare, while kind-hearted Kind tried to stop him. Then their sheep began to stray away and vanish, the closest-clipped first. The story is still being told by Snowflower’s magic chair. Vexation is annoyance. A cleft is a deep crack in a hillside, and to scour up it is to run up it fast. A moorland or heath is wild open land; a pasture is a grassy field. A countenance is a face.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from the flock melting away to the brothers finding the ancient shepherd; opens “"Kind grew tired of watching, and Clutch lost his sleep with vexation. The other…”; closes “…he had the countenance of one who had led a quiet life, and known no cares nor losses.”.

questions.prompt: How many sheep are left by spring? What does Clutch want to do with them?
facilitatorNotes: Three old, lame ewes; he wants to shear even them, though it is still cold.
evidence: Brother, there is wool to be had on their backs.

questions.prompt: Where does Kind look for comfort, and what does he see there?
facilitatorNotes: Up at the great hills at sunset, and he sees three sheep-like creatures run up a cleft as fast as deer.
evidence: three creatures like sheep scoured up a cleft in one of them as fleet as any deer

questions.prompt: Why does Clutch decide to leave the plain? Why does Kind go too?
facilitatorNotes: Clutch will not stay to be looked down on for being poor. Kind would rather farm, but goes to keep his brother company.
evidence: I'll not stay on this plain to be despised for poverty.
he resolved to bear him company

questions.prompt: What happens to the brothers when they hear the music? What do they find at the top?
facilitatorNotes: Their sore feet and heavy hearts are healed, and they follow it to a violet pasture of white sheep and an old shepherd with snow-white hair and beard. Ask what makes it feel magical.
evidence: the soreness passed from their feet, and the heaviness from their hearts

readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 3: Shearing the wolves
readings.challenge: Listen to each brother answer the old shepherd, and who is brave when it matters.
readings.focus: A strange test shows which brother is the true shepherd, and the lost flock comes home.
readings.context: Recap: greedy Clutch clipped his sheep bare, and one by one the whole flock vanished. With nothing left, Clutch and his gentle brother Kind climbed the hills, where music led them to a violet pasture, white sheep, and a very old shepherd. The story is still being told by Snowflower’s magic chair. A wallet here is a bag for food. Leathern means made of leather. Shaggy means with long, rough hair. Fleece is a sheep’s wool. Little-worth means not worth much.
readings.contentNote: A pack of howling wolves shows its teeth, and Clutch fears they will eat the brothers. No one is hurt.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from Kind greeting the ancient shepherd to the end of the chair’s story; opens “"'Good father,' said Kind, for his eldest brother hung back and was afraid, 'tell us what…”; closes “…till this day, but Clutch has grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears."”.

questions.prompt: How does Clutch describe himself when the old man asks who can shear best?
facilitatorNotes: As the closest shearer in all the plain, who leaves not enough wool for a thread; the boast he is proud of.
evidence: I am the closest shearer in all the plain country

questions.prompt: Who is the flock Clutch must shear? What does he do?
facilitatorNotes: A troop of shaggy wolves. He throws down the shears and hides behind the old man.
evidence: Clutch was glad to throw down his shears, and run behind the old man for safety

questions.prompt: How does Kind shear the wolves? Why do they stand still for him?
facilitatorNotes: Neatly but not too close, the way he wanted the sheep sheared. They seem to know him; they turn out to be his own lost sheep.
evidence: Kind clipped neatly, but not too close
the wild creature seemed to know him

questions.prompt: At the end, Clutch has “grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears.” Is this a happy ending for Clutch too?
facilitatorNotes: Yes and no: he loses the flock to his brother and becomes the helper, but he gets home, is welcomed, and grows less greedy. Some children will say he got off lightly; others that losing his pride was enough.
evidence: Clutch has grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears

readings.title: Childe Charity — Part 1: The beggar at the backdoor
readings.challenge: Notice how each person treats the old woman at the backdoor, and what Childe Charity gives up for her.
readings.focus: A proud family looks down on an orphan girl, who shares her supper and her bed with a beggar no one else will help.
readings.context: From Frances Browne’s Granny’s Wonderful Chair (1857), a book of fairy tales. A girl named Snowflower has a magic chair that tells stories when she asks it, and this is one of them. Because the chair is speaking, every paragraph begins with a quotation mark, and the people in the story speak inside single quotation marks. An orphan is a child whose parents have died. Childe is an old word for a well-born child, and charity means kindness and giving to people in need. A dowry was money a bride brought to her marriage. Civilly means politely. Humble means not proud, and a disposition is the way someone usually is. A dairy is where milk, butter and cheese are made; a garret is an attic room, and lumber here means old stored junk. To scour is to scrub hard. Granaries store grain. Condescended means came down from his pride. Victuals (say “vittles”) are food, and broken victuals are scraps. A herd-boy looks after cattle.
readings.contentNote: The old beggar woman is described as ugly, with a squinting eye, a club foot and crooked fingers; a servant calls her a witch and another throws her a bone. The story is on the side of the girl who is kind to her. The harvest supper has barrels of ale.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Story of Childe Charity,” from the start to the old woman leaving without a thank-you; opens “"Once upon a time, there lived in the west country a little girl who had neither father…”; closes “…girl awoke, she was up and gone, without so much as saying thank you, or good morning.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the rich family look down on Childe Charity?
facilitatorNotes: She has no money, and she is humble and kind, above all to people who are needy or despised. Her uncle will not call her his niece and her cousins will not keep her company.
evidence: partly because she had no fortune, and partly because of her humble, kindly disposition

questions.prompt: Where does Childe Charity sleep, and how well does she sleep there?
facilitatorNotes: In the back garret among junk and dried herbs, yet “as sound as a princess” in a palace. Ask what that tells you about her.
evidence: every night she slept in the back garret as sound as a princess could in her palace chamber

questions.prompt: What do the kitchen-maid, the herd-boy and Childe Charity each do when the old woman comes?
facilitatorNotes: The kitchen-maid sends her off as an ugly witch; the herd-boy throws her a bone; Childe Charity gives her own supper and bed, and scrapes the pots and sleeps on a sack herself.
evidence: she ordered her to be gone for an ugly witch
he threw her a bone over his shoulder

questions.prompt: The old woman never says thank you. Should Childe Charity mind? Would you?
facilitatorNotes: She does not seem to: she helps because the woman needs it, not for thanks. Many children will say they would mind, which is honest. Ask whether a kindness needs a thank-you to count.
evidence: without so much as saying thank you, or good morning

readings.title: Childe Charity — Part 2: The ugly dog
readings.challenge: Count how many nights the old woman comes, and listen for the strange thing the servants notice.
readings.focus: The old woman leaves a cross, ugly dog in Childe Charity’s care, and strange lights shine in the garret at night.
readings.context: Recap: Childe Charity, an orphan, works in the dairy of her proud, rich uncle’s farm and sleeps in the back garret. At a harvest supper a poor, ugly old woman begged at the backdoor, and only Childe Charity took her in, giving up her own supper and bed. The story is still being told by Snowflower’s magic chair. To make game of someone is to make fun of them. Genteel means grand and well-mannered, said here as a joke. To fawn on someone is to be loving to them, as a dog wags and licks. The shortest day of the year comes in December, just before Christmas. To count for something is to settle what is owed.
readings.contentNote: The proud cousins want the ugly dog drowned; Childe Charity keeps him safe.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Story of Childe Charity,” from the old woman’s return to the light and voices in the back garret; opens “"That day all the servants were sick after the feast, and mostly cross too—so you may…”; closes “…the Christmas fire, and heard voices like those of lords and ladies in the back garret.”.

questions.prompt: How many nights does the old woman come? What does she complain about?
facilitatorNotes: Nine nights in all. She asks why the bed is not softer and the blankets thicker, and still never says thank you.
evidence: why don't you make this bed softer? and why are your blankets so thin?

questions.prompt: What does the old woman leave with Childe Charity, and until when?
facilitatorNotes: An ugly, cross, ash-coloured dog that nobody else will keep, until the shortest day of the year, when they will “count for his keeping.”
evidence: I leave him to your care till the shortest day in all the year

questions.prompt: How does the dog behave with Childe Charity, and with everyone else? Why might that be?
facilitatorNotes: He fawns on her and snarls at everyone else; perhaps he knows who is kind to him. Some children will guess already that the dog is more than he seems.
evidence: The ugly dog began to fawn upon her, but he snarled at everybody else.

questions.prompt: What do the servants see and hear in the back garret at night? Why doesn’t Childe Charity know about it?
facilitatorNotes: A light brighter than a Christmas fire and voices like lords and ladies; she sleeps soundly through it all. Ask the child to guess what is going on.
evidence: they saw a light brighter and clearer than the Christmas fire, and heard voices like those of lords and ladies in the back garret

readings.title: Childe Charity — Part 3: Little men and little ladies
readings.challenge: Notice who creeps to the crack in the door each night, and what each one sees and hears.
readings.focus: Three watchers find out that the ugly dog is a royal prince, and that a stranger from the house is to be taken to a feast.
readings.context: Recap: an ugly old beggar woman came nine nights to the backdoor, and only Childe Charity took her in. Then the old woman left a cross, ugly dog in the girl’s care until the shortest day of the year. At night the servants saw a bright light and heard grand voices in the back garret where she sleeps beside the dog. A crevice is a narrow crack. Bugles are small trumpets. Crimson is deep red. To make reverence, or a courtesy, is to bow or curtsy. “Your highness” is how a prince is spoken to. A banquet is a feast, and tapestry is a woven picture hung on a wall. A wench is an old word for a girl or servant, and durst means dared.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Story of Childe Charity,” from the parlour-maid watching at the door to the master’s night of watching; opens “"Partly from fear, and partly from laziness, none of the servants would rise to see what…”; closes “…the straw, Childe Charity turned in her sleep, and the moon shone in on the back garret.”.

questions.prompt: Who watches at the door, night after night?
facilitatorNotes: First the little parlour-maid, then the aunt (the mistress), then the uncle (the master). Each laughs at the one before, then goes to see.
evidence: the little parlour-maid, who did least work and got most favour, because she gathered news for her mistress
that night the master thought he would like to see what went on in the back garret

questions.prompt: What do the little men and little ladies call the dog? What does that tell you?
facilitatorNotes: “Royal prince.” The ugly dog is really a fairy prince.
evidence: Royal prince, we have prepared the banquet hall.

questions.prompt: The dog keeps speaking of a stranger who has never feasted in their halls. Who do you think it is?
facilitatorNotes: Someone from this house; he does not say who. Most children will guess Childe Charity; ask them why. The story has not said yet.
evidence: a stranger who never feasted in our halls before

questions.prompt: The aunt calls the maid silly, and the uncle calls his wife foolish, yet each goes to look. What does that show about this family?
facilitatorNotes: Each is proud and thinks the others foolish, but each is curious and hopes there is something worth having. They look down even on one another. Some children will say anyone would want to see for themselves.
evidence: her mistress called her a silly wench to have such foolish dreams
he laughed at her for a foolish woman

readings.title: Childe Charity — Part 4: The shortest day
readings.challenge: Notice whom the uncle expects the fairies to take, and whom they take instead.
readings.focus: On the shortest day the beggar and her dog turn out to be a fairy princess and prince, and the kind girl rides away to Fairyland.
readings.context: Recap: Childe Charity, an orphan treated as a servant in her proud uncle’s house, took in an old beggar woman for nine nights and cared for her ugly dog. Watching at night, the maid, the aunt and the uncle each saw tiny lords and ladies call the dog “Royal prince” and prepare a feast for a stranger from the house. Of great account means very important. Mutton is sheep’s meat. Finery is fancy clothes, and gilding a thin coat of gold. A wager is a bet. Primroses are pale yellow spring flowers. Ivory is a creamy white material. To alight is to step down from a carriage.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Story of Childe Charity,” from the master’s sleepless night to the end of the chair’s story; opens “"The master could not close his eyes any more than the maid or the mistress, for thinking…”; closes “…and scoured no more, for she grew a great lady, even in the eyes of her proud cousins."”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the uncle think the fairies will take, and what does he do about it?
facilitatorNotes: One of his own daughters, because they are handsome and finely dressed. He takes the dog roast mutton, which the dog will not touch, and tells the girls to dress in their best.
evidence: he was sure it must be one of his daughters—they were so handsome, and had such fine clothes

questions.prompt: What happens to the old woman and the dog in the chariot?
facilitatorNotes: She turns into a beautiful young princess and he into a fair young prince. Their ugliness was a disguise.
evidence: the ugly old woman turned at once to a beautiful young princess

questions.prompt: What was the fairies’ wager, and how did Childe Charity settle it?
facilitatorNotes: Whether there were still good people in these false and greedy times. The princess said yes and won. Childe Charity proved it by being kind to a rude beggar and an ugly dog, never knowing she was being tested. Ask whether she would have been kind if she had known.
evidence: whether or not there were good people still to be found in these false and greedy times

questions.prompt: At the end Childe Charity is a great lady “even in the eyes of her proud cousins.” Have the cousins changed, or only what they can see?
facilitatorNotes: Many children will say only the gold and jewels changed their minds: they still judge people by riches. Others may hope they learned something. Childe Charity herself was the same girl all along.
evidence: she grew a great lady, even in the eyes of her proud cousins
